Genetic Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy

Genetic MONDO:0100062 Pathograph 79 Show in embeddings browser Epilepsy Neurodevelopmental Disorder

Genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) is a broad, genetically heterogeneous umbrella group of severe early-onset epilepsy syndromes in which pathogenic variants in any of more than nine hundred genes cause both refractory seizures and developmental impairment that exceeds what would be expected from the epileptic activity alone. Under the 2017 ILAE classification, "developmental and epileptic encephalopathy" recognizes two overlapping but separable contributors to the encephalopathy: a developmental component intrinsic to the underlying genetic etiology, and an epileptic component in which frequent seizures and epileptiform activity themselves worsen cognitive and behavioral outcome. Individual monogenic forms (numbered DEE1-DEE121+ in OMIM/MONDO, e.g. SCN1A-related Dravet syndrome, STXBP1 encephalopathy, KCNQ2-DEE, SCN2A-DEE, SCN8A-DEE, CDKL5 deficiency disorder, SYNGAP1-related DEE) are curated as their own dismech entries; this entry captures the mechanisms, phenotypic core, and clinical approach shared across the umbrella group. Modelling note: this is deliberately curated as an umbrella Disease rather than a Grouping over the gene-specific entries. A Grouping cannot carry pathophysiology, and the shared two-component DEE mechanism - the very thing that makes DEE a coherent concept - is the primary content here. The existing Epilepsy and Diabetes_Mellitus entries set the same precedent. Gene-specific detail (variant spectra, gene-specific EEG signatures, per-gene natural history and treatment response) belongs on the child entries, not here. Numbered forms that do not yet have a dismech entry of their own are enumerated in has_subtypes instead, each anchored to its MONDO term and to its causal gene, so that the concept and the gene are both recorded until a full entry exists. A subtype row is therefore a placeholder for a child entry, not a substitute for one.

Inheritance

3
Autosomal dominant inheritance HP:0000006
Genetic DEE is most commonly regarded as a de novo dominant disease class, and the highest-prevalence individual entities (SCN1A, SCN2A, STXBP1, KCNQ2, SCN8A) are indeed de novo autosomal dominant, so affected children typically have unaffected parents. Parental germline mosaicism gives a small but non-zero sibling recurrence risk. Note that this reflects the distribution of *cases*: counted by *gene*, more DEE genes follow autosomal recessive than dominant inheritance.
Autosomal dominant inheritance
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:39237642 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Genetic DEEs are most commonly regarded as de novo dominant disorders ; however, more DEE genes follow autosomal recessive than dominant inheritance, with a small number following X-linked or mitochondrial inheritance patterns"
Establishes de novo dominant inheritance as the prevailing mode while making explicit the gene-count versus case-count distinction that this description records.
PMID:39613335 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in genes with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern occurred in 77% (n=1207) patients; 17% (n=271) in X-linked genes and 6% (n=90) in genes with autosomal recessive inheritance."
Quantifies the case-level distribution of inheritance modes across 1568 molecularly diagnosed genetic DEE patients, confirming autosomal dominant as the predominant mode by case count.
PMID:39237642 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Parental mosaicism places parents at an increased risk of having a second child with a DEE, as a small population of their sperm or ova carry the pathogenic variant."
Supports the non-zero sibling recurrence risk stated in this description, which would otherwise be an uncited claim.
Autosomal recessive inheritance HP:0000007
Counted by gene rather than by case, more DEE genes follow autosomal recessive than dominant inheritance. Biallelic forms are individually rarer but collectively numerous, and are enriched in consanguineous families and among metabolic and glycosylation-pathway DEE genes.
Autosomal recessive inheritance
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:39237642 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"more DEE genes follow autosomal recessive than dominant inheritance"
Directly supports autosomal recessive inheritance as the most common mode when DEE genes are counted individually.
PMID:39613335 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"6% (n=90) in genes with autosomal recessive inheritance."
Quantifies the autosomal recessive share of molecularly diagnosed genetic DEE cases, contrasting with its larger share of the gene count.
X-linked inheritance HP:0001417
A small number of genetic DEE genes are X-linked, including CDKL5, PCDH19, and ARX, together accounting for 17% of molecularly diagnosed cases. X-linked disease and mosaicism complicate cellular targeting for emerging gene therapies. PCDH19 departs from the usual X-linked pattern in that heterozygous females are affected while hemizygous males are typically unaffected transmitting carriers; that observation is recorded in the PCDH19 genetic entry, while its mechanistic explanation (cellular interference) is left to the PCDH19 Clustering Epilepsy child entry, since no source cached here states it.
X-linked inheritance
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:39237642 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"with a small number following X-linked or mitochondrial inheritance patterns"
Establishes X-linked inheritance as a recognized but numerically minor mode among DEE genes.
PMID:39613335 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"17% (n=271) in X-linked genes"
Quantifies the X-linked share of molecularly diagnosed genetic DEE cases.
PMID:39237642 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Mosaicism and X-linked disorders further complicate cellular targeting."
Supports the therapeutic-targeting caveat noted for X-linked genetic DEE.

Subtypes

51
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 6B, non-Dravet (SCN1A) MONDO:0030268
SCN1A hgnc:10585 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in SCN1A (hgnc:10585). hgnc:10585 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
The non-Dravet pole of SCN1A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. MONDO treats this as a class distinct from both Dravet syndrome and SCN1A DEE6A, and the founding cohort argues the same clinically: seizure onset at 6 to 12 weeks, profound developmental impairment with no speech and no ambulation, and a hyperkinetic movement disorder with prominent oral dyskinesia, a combination the authors describe as readily distinguishable from Dravet syndrome. Eight of the nine children carried the recurrent missense variant p.Thr226Met. Dravet syndrome itself is curated as the separate Dravet_syndrome entry, and SCN1A is carried in this entry's genetic section and wired to the ion-channel and synaptic lesion node, so this row records only the non-Dravet concept.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:28794249 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We describe a distinct SCN1A phenotype, early infantile SCN1A encephalopathy, which is readily distinguishable from the well-recognized entities of Dravet syndrome and genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus."
Establishes the non-Dravet SCN1A encephalopathy that this subtype term names, and its separation from Dravet syndrome.
PMID:28794249 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Seizure onset was at 6 to 12 weeks with hemiclonic seizures, bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, or spasms. All children had profound developmental impairment and were nonverbal and nonambulatory, and 7 of 9 required a gastrostomy."
Quantifies the onset window and the severity that distinguish this subtype from Dravet syndrome.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 23 (DOCK7) MONDO:0014371
DOCK7 hgnc:19190 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in DOCK7 (hgnc:19190). hgnc:19190 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
Biallelic truncating DOCK7 variants. The founding report described three girls from two nonconsanguineous families with dysmorphic features, early-onset intractable epilepsy, intellectual disability and cortical blindness, all compound heterozygous for truncating DOCK7 alleles. DOCK7 encodes a Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factor implicated in the genesis and polarization of newborn pyramidal neurons and in the morphological differentiation of cortical GABAergic interneurons, so the lesion is developmental rather than primarily one of channel conduction.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:24814191 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We describe here three girls from two nonconsanguineous families affected by a clinical entity characterized by dysmorphic features, early-onset intractable epilepsy, intellectual disability, and cortical blindness."
Establishes the DEE23 clinical entity, including the cortical blindness that distinguishes it.
PMID:24814191 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Sanger sequencing confirmed that all three individuals are compound heterozygotes for these truncating mutations in DOCK7."
Establishes biallelic truncating DOCK7 variants as the lesion defining this subtype.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 35 (ITPA) MONDO:0014719
ITPA hgnc:6176 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in ITPA (hgnc:6176). hgnc:6176 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
Inosine triphosphate pyrophosphohydrolase (ITPase) deficiency, a purine pathway defect. Reported as an infantile-onset epileptic encephalopathy with a lethal course: infantile-onset neurodegeneration, progressive microcephaly and epilepsy, with cardiomyopathy in 42% of those in whom it was explicitly evaluated. This subtype sits in the metabolic rather than the channelopathy arm of the DEE umbrella, and MONDO also files it under inborn disorder of purine metabolism.
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:35098521 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Inosine triphosphate pyrophosphohydrolase (ITPase) deficiency associated with mutations in the ITPA gene is a recently characterized purine pathway defect that presents with early infantile epileptic encephalopathy and lethal course."
Establishes ITPA as the causal gene and the early infantile epileptic encephalopathy phenotype.
PMID:35098521 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"ITPA-related encephalopathy presents with infantile-onset neurodegeneration, progressive microcephaly, and epilepsy."
Supports the microcephaly and neurodegenerative course recorded for this subtype.
PMID:35098521 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Cardiomyopathy was noted in 42% of patients where it was explicitly evaluated (n = 5/12)."
Source for the cardiomyopathy figure recorded in this subtype's description.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 36 (ALG13) MONDO:0010472
ALG13 hgnc:30881 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in ALG13 (hgnc:30881). hgnc:30881 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
X-linked ALG13-related DEE, in almost all reported cases caused by the recurrent de novo missense variant p.(Asn107Ser). In a 38-individual series 37 were girls and one was a boy. It usually manifests as West syndrome with severe to profound developmental delay. Transferrin electrophoresis is normal in most cases, and the cited series leaves open whether this is genuinely a congenital disorder of glycosylation, which is how MONDO classifies it.
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:33410528 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"X-linked ALG13-related DEE usually manifests as West syndrome with severe to profound developmental delay. It is predominantly caused by the recurrent de novo missense variant p.(Asn107Ser)."
Establishes the recurrent de novo ALG13 variant and the West syndrome presentation of this subtype.
PMID:33410528 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Comprehensive functional studies will be able to prove or disprove an association with congenital disorder of glycosylation."
Records that the glycosylation-disorder classification MONDO applies to this term is unsettled in the clinical literature.
PMID:33410528 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We delineate the phenotypic spectrum of 38 individuals, 37 girls and one boy, 16 of them novel and 22 published, with the most common pathogenic ALG13 variant p.(Asn107Ser) and additionally report the phenotype of three individuals carrying other likely pathogenic ALG13 variants."

Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 37 (FRRS1L) MONDO:0014859
FRRS1L hgnc:1362 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in FRRS1L (hgnc:1362). hgnc:1362 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
Biallelic loss-of-function FRRS1L variants. FRRS1L encodes an AMPA receptor outer-core protein, and its loss attenuates AMPA-mediated currents, so this is a postsynaptic glutamatergic lesion. The reported phenotype couples epilepsy with prominent choreoathetosis, which is why the founding report called it an epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:27236917 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We describe a neurological disorder with epilepsy and prominent choreoathetosis caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in FRRS1L, which encodes an AMPA receptor outer-core protein."
Establishes biallelic FRRS1L variants and the epileptic-dyskinetic phenotype of this subtype.
PMID:27236917 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Loss of FRRS1L function attenuates AMPA-mediated currents, implicating chronic abnormalities of glutamatergic neurotransmission in this monogenic neurological disease of childhood."
Supports placing the FRRS1L lesion in the synaptic arm of the DEE mechanism.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 48 (AP3B2) MONDO:0015000
AP3B2 hgnc:567 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in AP3B2 (hgnc:567). hgnc:567 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
Biallelic AP3B2 variants. AP3B2 encodes the neuron-specific beta subunit of the AP-3 vesicle coat adaptor complex; the ubiquitous isoform AP3B1 causes Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome type 2 instead, so the neuronal restriction of this subunit is what makes the AP3B2 phenotype purely neurological. Reverse phenotyping of twelve affected individuals from eight families gave a homogeneous early-onset epileptic encephalopathy with severe developmental delay, optic atrophy and postnatal microcephaly, and no albinism or haematological involvement.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:27889060 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Reverse phenotyping of 12 affected individuals from eight families revealed a homogeneous EOEE phenotype characterized by severe developmental delay, poor visual contact with optic atrophy, and postnatal microcephaly."
Establishes the DEE48 clinical entity and the optic atrophy that characterises it.
PMID:27889060 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Among a cohort of 57 individuals with epileptic encephalopathy, we ascertained two unrelated affected individuals with EOEE associated with developmental impairment and autosomal-recessive variants in AP3B2 by means of whole-exome sequencing."
Establishes autosomal-recessive AP3B2 variants as the lesion defining this subtype.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 51 (MDH2) MONDO:0015025
MDH2 hgnc:6971 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in MDH2 (hgnc:6971). hgnc:6971 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
Biallelic MDH2 variants, a Krebs cycle defect. MDH2 encodes mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase, which converts malate to oxaloacetate. The three unrelated subjects of the founding report had early-onset generalised hypotonia, psychomotor delay and refractory epilepsy with raised lactate in blood and cerebrospinal fluid; their fibroblasts showed loss of MDH2 protein with enzymatic activity close to null, and accumulation of malate and fumarate. The lesion is therefore metabolic rather than one of channel conduction, which is why this subtype gene is wired to the non-channelopathy lesion node.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:27989324 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We report bi-allelic pathogenic mutations in MDH2 in three unrelated subjects presenting with early-onset generalized hypotonia, psychomotor delay, refractory epilepsy, and elevated lactate in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid."
Establishes the DEE51 clinical entity and biallelic MDH2 variants as its lesion.
PMID:27989324 SUPPORT In Vitro
"Functional studies in fibroblasts from affected subjects showed both an apparently complete loss of MDH2 levels and MDH2 enzymatic activity close to null."
Shows the lesion abolishes malate dehydrogenase activity, which is the mechanism this subtype contributes.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 53 (SYNJ1) MONDO:0033362
SYNJ1 hgnc:11503 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in SYNJ1 (hgnc:11503). hgnc:11503 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
Biallelic SYNJ1 variants. SYNJ1 encodes synaptojanin 1, a polyphosphoinositide phosphatase with two consecutive phosphatase domains that acts in synaptic vesicle dynamics. The allelic series separates two diseases: variants that selectively abolish only the Sac1 domain cause early-onset parkinsonism, whereas a critical reduction of the dual phosphatase activity causes this neonatal refractory epilepsy with progressive neurological decline. A screen of 543 further patients with epilepsy and intellectual disability found no additional pathogenic variants, so SYNJ1 deficiency is rare and tied to a specific phenotype.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:27435091 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We performed whole exome or genome sequencing in three independent sib pairs with early onset refractory seizures and progressive neurological decline, and identified novel segregating recessive SYNJ1 defects."
Establishes the DEE53 clinical entity and recessive SYNJ1 variants as its lesion.
PMID:27435091 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"A genetic follow-up screening in a large cohort of 543 patients with a wide phenotypical range of epilepsies and intellectual disability revealed no additional pathogenic variants, showing that SYNJ1 deficiency is rare and probably linked to a specific phenotype."
Sources the rarity and phenotypic specificity stated in this row description.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 57 (KCNT2) MONDO:0033366
KCNT2 hgnc:18866 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in KCNT2 (hgnc:18866). hgnc:18866 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
De novo KCNT2 variants. KCNT2 encodes a sodium-activated potassium channel subunit of the same subfamily as KCNT1. The two girls of the founding report had West syndrome evolving to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in one and epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures in the other. In vitro analysis indicated quinidine-responsive gain of function, and quinidine add-on therapy produced marked clinical improvement in one of them, so this subtype shares the pharmacological profile as well as the phenotype of KCNT1-related disease.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:29740868 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We report on 2 females with de novo variants in KCNT2 with West syndrome followed by Lennox-Gastaut syndrome or with DEE with migrating focal seizures."
Establishes the DEE57 clinical entity and de novo KCNT2 variants as its lesion.
PMID:29740868 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"After in vitro analysis suggested quinidine-responsive gain-of-function effects, we treated 1 of the girls with quinidine add-on therapy and achieved marked clinical improvements."
Sources both the gain-of-function mechanism and the quinidine response stated in this row description.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 58 (NTRK2) MONDO:0033367
NTRK2 hgnc:8032 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in NTRK2 (hgnc:8032). hgnc:8032 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
NTRK2-related DEE, reported with a recurrent variant in four of the five cases in the cited series. The phenotype is early-onset seizures beginning as infantile spasms and later evolving to multifocal seizures, with global developmental delay, variable movement disorders, microcephaly and optic nerve hypoplasia. HGNC names NTRK2 neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase 2, with TRKB as an alias symbol, so the lesion is in receptor signalling rather than in channel conduction.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:34425480 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Five cases of NTRK2-related DEE were identified. Four had a previously described recurrent variant in NTRK2 and one had a novel variant."
Establishes NTRK2 as the causal gene of this subtype and the recurrence of one variant.
PMID:34425480 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"The phenotype was characterized by early-onset seizures (infantile spasms, later evolving to multifocal seizures), global developmental delay, variable movement disorders, microcephaly and optic nerve hypoplasia."
Source for the seizure evolution, microcephaly and optic nerve hypoplasia recorded here.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 59 (GABBR2) MONDO:0033368
GABBR2 hgnc:4507 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in GABBR2 (hgnc:4507). hgnc:4507 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
De novo GABBR2 variants. GABBR2 encodes the type 2 subunit of the metabotropic GABA-B receptor, so this subtype sits with the GABA-A receptor subunit subtypes as a lesion of GABAergic inhibition rather than of a voltage-gated channel. De novo GABBR2 mutations were reported in two individuals in the combined EuroEPINOMICS and Epi4K/EPGP trio cohort, which treated them as suggestive rather than statistically established; a later whole-genome study of unexplained DEE provided the causal link.
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:25262651 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"In this expanded cohort, we find 429 de novo mutations, including de novo mutations in DNM1 in five individuals and de novo mutations in GABBR2, FASN, and RYR3 in two individuals each."
The first observation of de novo GABBR2 mutations in a DEE trio cohort, which is the report OMIM cites for DEE59.
PMID:25262651 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We bring statistical evidence that mutations in DNM1 cause epileptic encephalopathy, find suggestive evidence for a role of three additional genes, and show that at least 12% of analyzed individuals have an identifiable causal de novo mutation."
Sources the statement that the first report treated GABBR2 as suggestive rather than established; the statistical evidence in that paper is for DNM1, not for GABBR2.
PMID:29100083 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"By combining these strategies, we were able to provide a causal link between DEE and the following genes: NTRK2, GABRB2, CLTC, DHDDS, NUS1, RAB11A, GABBR2, and SNAP25."
Establishes GABBR2 as causal for DEE. The sentence names eight genes, so it supports gene-disease causality for each named gene and no gene-specific phenotype claim.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 60 (CNPY3) MONDO:0033369
CNPY3 hgnc:11968 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in CNPY3 (hgnc:11968). hgnc:11968 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
Biallelic CNPY3 variants. CNPY3 encodes an endoplasmic reticulum co-chaperone that regulates the subcellular distribution and responses of multiple Toll-like receptors, a function outside the channel and synaptic classes. The three individuals of the founding report presented as West syndrome and all three had hippocampal malrotation; CNPY3 protein was severely reduced in lymphoblastoid cells from two of them. Cnpy3-knockout mice showed spastic or dystonic features at rest and enhanced resting EEG activity in the fast beta band, which the authors suggest could mimic the fast waves seen in those two individuals.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:29394991 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We have now identified biallelic CNPY3 variants in three individuals with WS; these include compound-heterozygous missense and frameshift variants in a family with two affected siblings (individuals 1 and 2) and a homozygous splicing variant in a consanguineous family (individual 3)."
Establishes the DEE60 clinical entity, presenting as West syndrome, and biallelic CNPY3 variants as its lesion.
PMID:29394991 SUPPORT Model Organism
"Cnpy3-knockout mice exhibited spastic or dystonic features under resting conditions and hyperactivity and anxiolytic behavior during the open field test."

Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 61 (ADAM22) MONDO:0033370
ADAM22 hgnc:201 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in ADAM22 (hgnc:201). hgnc:201 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
Biallelic inactivating ADAM22 variants. ADAM22 is the postsynaptic receptor for the secreted protein LGI1, and this subtype is the recessive counterpart of the dominant LGI1 epilepsy with auditory features. All affected individuals in the cited series had infantile-onset treatment-resistant epilepsy. Transfected-cell studies indicated three distinct pathological mechanisms: defective cell-membrane expression, impaired LGI1 binding, and impaired interaction with the postsynaptic density protein PSD-95.

PMID:35373813 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We refine the phenotype and report 19 additional individuals harbouring compound heterozygous or homozygous inactivating ADAM22 variants, of whom 18 had clinical data available."
Establishes biallelic inactivating ADAM22 variants in a cohort, defining this subtype.
PMID:35373813 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"All affected individuals exhibited infantile-onset, treatment-resistant epilepsy."
Source for the uniform infantile-onset drug-resistant epilepsy recorded here.
PMID:35373813 SUPPORT In Vitro
"Functional studies in transfected cell lines confirmed the deleteriousness of all identified variants and indicated at least three distinct pathological mechanisms: (i) defective cell membrane expression; (ii) impaired LGI1-binding; and/or (iii) impaired interaction with the postsynaptic density..."

Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 62 (SCN3A) MONDO:0033371
SCN3A hgnc:10590 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in SCN3A (hgnc:10590). hgnc:10590 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
De novo SCN3A variants. SCN3A encodes the Nav1.3 sodium channel alpha subunit, highly expressed in brain and, before this report, not linked to early infantile epileptic encephalopathy. The four patients carried heterozygous de novo missense variants, and recordings showed gain of channel function with a markedly increased slowly inactivating current; phenytoin and lacosamide blocked that slowly inactivating component selectively, which is the pharmacological lead the authors draw from the mechanism. Variants known or presumed to be inherited did not show gain of function.

PMID:29466837 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Here, we describe a cohort of 4 patients with epileptic encephalopathy and heterozygous de novo missense variants in SCN3A (p.Ile875Thr in 2 cases, p.Pro1333Leu, and p.Val1769Ala)."

PMID:29466837 SUPPORT In Vitro
"Electrophysiological recordings of mutant channels revealed prominent gain of channel function, with a markedly increased amplitude of the slowly inactivating current component"

Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 67 (CUX2) MONDO:0029138
CUX2 hgnc:19347 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in CUX2 (hgnc:19347). hgnc:19347 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
The recurrent de novo CUX2 p.Glu590Lys variant. CUX2 is a cut homeodomain transcription factor with a role in dendrite branching, spine development and synapse formation in layer II to III cortical neurons, so the lesion is transcriptional rather than a channel or synaptic protein defect and the gene is wired to the non-channelopathy lesion node. The nine-patient cohort spans a phenotypic range with infantile-onset myoclonic DEE at the severe end and generalised epilepsy with severe static developmental encephalopathy at the milder end; the variant affects a highly conserved residue in the CUT domain predicted to interfere with DNA binding.

PMID:29630738 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"We identify a recurrent de novo CUX2 p.Glu590Lys as a novel genetic cause for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE)."
Establishes the DEE67 clinical entity and the recurrent CUX2 variant as its lesion.
PMID:29630738 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Patients with CUX2 p.Glu590Lys display a distinctive phenotypic spectrum, which is predominantly generalized epilepsy, with infantile-onset myoclonic DEE at the severe end and generalized epilepsy with severe static developmental encephalopathy at the milder end of the spectrum."

Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 68 (TRAK1) MONDO:0032598
TRAK1 hgnc:29947 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in TRAK1 (hgnc:29947). hgnc:29947 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
Biallelic truncating TRAK1 variants. The founding report identified a homozygous splice variant in six lethal encephalopathic patients from three unrelated families; patient-derived fibroblasts showed irregular mitochondrial distribution, altered mitochondrial motility, reduced membrane potential and diminished respiration. Note that the founding report frames the phenotype as a fatal encephalopathy rather than using the DEE label that OMIM 618201 and MONDO later attached to this locus.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:28364549 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Using whole exome sequencing, we identified homozygous truncating variants in TRAK1 (NM_001042646:c.287-2A > C), in six lethal encephalopathic patients from three unrelated families."
Establishes the biallelic TRAK1 lesion and the lethal encephalopathic phenotype of this subtype.
PMID:28364549 SUPPORT In Vitro
"In comparison with normal cells, TRAK1-deficient fibroblasts showed irregular mitochondrial distribution, altered mitochondrial motility, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, and diminished mitochondrial respiration."
Source for the mitochondrial trafficking and respiration defect; the measurements are in patient-derived fibroblasts.
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 70 (PHACTR1) MONDO:0032663
PHACTR1 hgnc:20990 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this subtype is caused by variation in this gene This subtype is caused by variation in PHACTR1 (hgnc:20990). hgnc:20990 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
De novo PHACTR1 variants, whose founding report is titled for their identification in West syndrome. ⚙

Pathophysiology

7
Genetic Lesion in an Ion Channel or Synaptic Gene
A de novo or inherited pathogenic variant in one of a large and growing set of genes encoding voltage-gated ion channels (e.g. SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, KCNA2, KCNT1, CACNA1E, HCN1), presynaptic vesicle-cycle and neurotransmitter-release machinery (STXBP1, DNM1, SNAP25, CPLX1, UNC13A), postsynaptic glutamate or GABA receptors (GRIN1, GRIN2A, GRIN2B, GABRA1, GABRB3), or chromatin/transcriptional regulators active in neurodevelopment (CDKL5, FOXG1, CHD2) disrupts normal neuronal excitability or synaptic signaling. Gene-defined subtypes wired at this node in this entry, beyond the examples above, are CACNA2D1 (the alpha-2-delta-1 auxiliary subunit of CaV1 and CaV2 voltage-gated calcium channels), FGF13/FHF2 (an intracellular regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels), SV2A (a synaptic vesicle glycoprotein and the binding site of levetiracetam), FRRS1L (an AMPA receptor outer-core protein), LGI1 together with its postsynaptic receptor ADAM22, BAIAP2 (dendritic spine morphogenesis and excitatory synapse formation), and ACTL6B (a subunit of the neuron-specific chromatin remodelling complex nBAF). Each functional assignment is taken from the publication cited on that subtype's own has_subtypes row. The DEE-series subtypes added under this parent extend that list with four further voltage-gated channel subunits (SCN3A/Nav1.3, KCNC2/Kv3.2, KCNH5/EAG2-Kv10.2, and the sodium-activated potassium channel KCNT2); the stretch-activated channel TMEM63B; four GABA receptor subunits, namely the GABA-A subunits GABRB2, GABRA2 and GABRA5 together with the metabotropic GABA-B subunit GABBR2; the vesicular GABA transporter SLC32A1; and three further components of the presynaptic vesicle cycle, namely the AAA ATPase NSF, which acts in SNARE complex assembly and disassembly, its beta attachment protein NAPB, and the polyphosphoinositide phosphatase SYNJ1.

Downstream
Neuronal Excitation-Inhibition Imbalance The gene-level lesion alters neuronal excitability or synaptic signalling, shifting the excitation-inhibition balance of the network.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:39237642 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"900 genes have been identified as monogenic causes of DEEs and many cell components and processes"
Establishes the extreme monogenic heterogeneity of the DEE umbrella, the defining upstream trigger of this entry.
PMID:35951482 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Genetic DEEs have been associated with mutations in many genes involved in different functions including cell migration, proliferation, and organization, neuronal excitability, and synapse transmission and plasticity."
Enumerates the functional gene classes affected, matching the ion-channel, synaptic, and neurodevelopmental categories described in this node.
Neuronal Excitation-Inhibition Imbalance
Depending on the specific gene and variant, the molecular lesion produces either a gain- or loss-of-function shift in neuronal excitability (e.g. gain-of-function SCN2A/SCN8A sodium-channel variants causing neuronal hyperexcitability versus loss-of-function SCN1A variants preferentially impairing GABAergic interneuron firing), converging on a common circuit-level disruption of the balance between excitatory and inhibitory synaptic drive.
GABAergic interneuron CL:0000617 Cell Ontology (CL) Relation: this pathophysiological event involves this cell type This pathophysiological event involves GABAergic interneuron, annotated with GABAergic neuron (CL:0000617). CL:0000617 is a cell type from the Cell Ontology.
GABA Signaling Pathway GO:0007214 Gene Ontology (GO) Relation: this pathophysiological event involves this biological process This pathophysiological event involves decreased GABA Signaling Pathway, annotated with gamma-aminobutyric acid signaling pathway (GO:0007214). GO:0007214 is a biological process from the Gene Ontology. ↓ DECREASED
Downstream
Hypersynchronous Network Activity and Seizures Excitation-inhibition imbalance drives the seizure arm of the DEE mechanism.
Impaired Synaptic Maturation and Neurodevelopment The same molecular lesion independently disrupts circuit maturation, producing the developmental arm.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:39858526 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Many genes mutated in DEEs encode ion channels, causing current conduction disruptions known as channelopathies."
Supports the channelopathy arm in which the genetic lesion alters neuronal excitability, the proximate cause of excitation-inhibition imbalance.
Hypersynchronous Network Activity and Seizures
Excitation-inhibition imbalance produces hypersynchronous, epileptiform cortical network activity, manifesting clinically as frequent, often multiple, drug-resistant seizure types with an abnormal interictal EEG background.
neuron CL:0000540 Cell Ontology (CL) Relation: this pathophysiological event involves this cell type This pathophysiological event involves neuron (CL:0000540). CL:0000540 is a cell type from the Cell Ontology.
Action Potential GO:0001508 Gene Ontology (GO) Relation: this pathophysiological event involves this biological process This pathophysiological event involves increased Action Potential (GO:0001508). GO:0001508 is a biological process from the Gene Ontology. ↑ INCREASED
Downstream
Drug-Resistant Seizures The hypersynchronous network state is what is observed clinically as the antiseizure-medication-refractory seizures that the ILAE operational definition puts at the centre of the DEE concept.
Status Epilepticus Status epilepticus is the failure of a seizure to self-terminate. Convulsive status epilepticus was recorded in 47 per cent and nonconvulsive status epilepticus in 19 per cent of a 510-patient genetic DEE cohort.
Abnormal EEG Background The same hypersynchrony is recorded interictally as frequent epileptiform activity on an abnormal EEG background, which is the electrographic rather than the clinical reading of this node.
Epileptic Encephalopathy Component Ongoing seizures and epileptiform activity themselves degrade cognitive and behavioural function.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:40013914 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are the most severe group of epilepsies, characterized by drug-resistant seizures and developmental slowing or regression."
The ILAE operational definition identifies drug-resistant seizures as a defining clinical output of the DEE network mechanism.
Impaired Synaptic Maturation and Neurodevelopment
Independent of seizure activity, the same channel or synaptic-gene defect disrupts activity-dependent synaptic pruning, circuit maturation, and neuronal migration/connectivity during critical developmental windows, producing a developmental encephalopathy component that is not fully reversible by seizure control alone.
Downstream
Developmental Encephalopathy Component Disrupted circuit maturation yields developmental delay and intellectual disability independently of seizure burden.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:39858526 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"many other mechanisms have been identified: impaired neurogenesis, metabolic disorders, disruption of dendrite and axon growth, maintenance and synapse formation abnormalities -synaptopathies."
Documents the non-channelopathy, neurodevelopmental mechanisms that constitute this seizure-independent arm of the DEE mechanism.
Epileptic Encephalopathy Component
Frequent seizures and ongoing epileptiform discharges themselves contribute to cognitive slowing, developmental regression, and behavioral disturbance, over and above the effect of the underlying genetic lesion. This component can partially improve with effective seizure control.
Downstream
Developmental Regression What this component adds is deterioration: worsening of development on a background of established impairment, rather than the delay itself. That is why loss of previously acquired skills is routed from here rather than from the developmental component, which the entry treats as the source of the delay.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:35951482 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"on a background of developmental impairment that tends to worsen as a consequence of epilepsy"
States the epileptic-encephalopathy component explicitly: the epilepsy itself worsens developmental impairment.
PMID:28276062 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"New terminology is introduced such as developmental and epileptic encephalopathy."
The 2017 ILAE classification introduced the DEE term precisely to separate the epileptic from the developmental contribution to the encephalopathy.
Developmental Encephalopathy Component
Developmental delay, intellectual disability, and often autistic features that arise directly from the genetic etiology's disruption of neurodevelopment, and that may be present even before seizure onset or persist despite adequate seizure control.
Downstream
Developmental Delay Delayed acquisition of milestones is the direct expression of this component, and in the DEE concept it may precede seizure onset.
Intellectual Disability The cognitive endpoint of the developmental arm. Its features may persist despite adequate seizure control, which is the clinical observation that makes this arm separable from the epileptic one.
Autistic Behavior Autistic features are routed from the developmental rather than the epileptic arm because they are part of the cognitive and behavioural phenotype of the underlying genetic lesion. The sources cited here name autism spectrum disorder and behavioural deficits as features of the DEE group without attributing them to either arm, so the routing is this entry's model rather than a claim either source makes.
Movement Disorder Movement disorders are routed from the developmental arm because most of the epilepsy-dyskinesia genes map to the same ion-channel and synaptic pathways as the upstream lesion nodes, rather than arising from the seizure burden. The cited review reports co-occurrence and gene-pathway membership; it does not test which arm produces the movement disorder, so this edge is an inference from the entry's two-component model.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:39858526 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"What sets DEEs apart is their complex interplay of epilepsy and developmental delay, often driven by genetic factors. These two aspects influence one another but can develop independently, creating diagnostic and therapeutic challenges."
Directly supports modeling the developmental component as a separate arm that can arise independently of the seizure burden - the conceptual basis for splitting these two nodes.
Genetic Lesion Beyond the Channelopathies
A large share of the genes in which pathogenic variants cause genetic DEE encode neither an ion channel nor a core synaptic protein, and the DEE literature explicitly separates these mechanisms from the channelopathies. The gene-defined subtypes wired at this node in this entry span Rac-GEF-dependent neuronal polarity (DOCK7), actin and protein-phosphatase-1 regulation in cortical migration (PHACTR1), receptor tyrosine kinase signalling (NTRK2), spliceosomal small nuclear RNA (RNU2-2), de-UFMylation (UFSP2), endoplasmic-reticulum stress signalling (RNF13), mitochondrial protein biosynthesis and mitochondrial trafficking (PARS2, TRAK1), purine metabolism and asparagine-linked glycosylation (ITPA, ALG13), endolysosomal acidification (ATP6V0A1), Na+/K+-ATPase pump function and neutral amino-acid transport (ATP1A2, SLC38A3), DNA repair (PNKP), and one gene in the 1q41-q42 microdeletion interval whose molecular function no reference cited here states (FBXO28). The DEE-series subtypes added under this parent extend that list with a Krebs cycle enzyme (MDH2), an endoplasmic-reticulum co-chaperone (CNPY3), a cut homeodomain transcription factor (CUX2), a cohesin subunit (SMC1A), a factor that targets arginine tRNAs for 3-methylcytosine modification (DALRD3), the v-ATPase A subunit (ATP6V1A), a nucleocytoplasmic shuttling RNA-binding protein (CELF2), a trans-Golgi network protein required for peptide hormone processing (HID1), a microtubule-associated serine-threonine kinase (MAST3), an inhibitory component of the mTOR pathway (DEPDC5), the anaphase-promoting complex subunit Cdh1 (FZR1), an ESCRT-II subunit (SNF8), the BRCA1-associated ATM activator (BRAT1), and the neuron-specific beta subunit of the AP-3 vesicle coat adaptor (AP3B2). AP3B2 is placed here rather than at the synaptic node because the AP-3 complex acts in organelle and vesicle biogenesis rather than at the synapse itself. Each functional assignment is taken from the publication cited on that subtype's own has_subtypes row. The node is kept separate from the ion-channel and synaptic lesion node because the two classes reach the shared excitation-inhibition and neurodevelopmental arms by different routes, not because the subtypes here are milder.

Downstream
Impaired Synaptic Maturation and Neurodevelopment A lesion in metabolic, transport, proteostasis, RNA-processing, cytoskeletal or genome-maintenance machinery disrupts circuit maturation directly, producing the developmental arm without requiring a primary change in channel conduction.
Neuronal Excitation-Inhibition Imbalance The same non-channel lesions also reach excitation-inhibition balance, either by limiting the supply of neurotransmitter precursors and the ion gradients that neuronal firing depends on, or by altering neuronal excitability directly.

Medical Actions

Anti-Seizure Medication
Action: PharmacotherapyNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is Pharmacotherapy (NCIT:C15986). NCIT:C15986 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. NCIT:C15986
Agent: anticonvulsant agent NCIT:C264 NCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment uses this therapeutic agent This treatment uses anticonvulsant agent (NCIT:C264). NCIT:C264 is a therapeutic agent from the NCI Thesaurus.
Platform: Small molecule
Broad-spectrum and gene-informed anti-seizure medication selection, guided where possible by the specific ion-channel gain- versus loss-of-function mechanism (e.g. sodium-channel blockers are often beneficial in SCN2A/SCN8A gain-of-function DEE but can worsen seizures in SCN1A-related Dravet syndrome loss-of-function disease).
Mechanism Target:
INHIBITS Hypersynchronous Network Activity and Seizures — Antiseizure medication suppresses the seizure-generating network activity. Which agent helps versus harms is determined by the upstream channel lesion: sodium-channel blockers benefit SCN2A/SCN8A gain-of-function disease but worsen SCN1A loss-of-function Dravet syndrome.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:39237642 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Understanding the functional consequences of the SCN1A pathogenic variant informs management, as some sodium channel blocker (SCB) antiseizure medications (ASMs) may exacerbate seizures in Dravet syndrome, whereas patients with the non-Dravet, EIDEE phenotype due to GOF variants may respond to..."
Directly supports the gain- versus loss-of-function prescribing logic stated in this mechanism description: sodium-channel blockers exacerbate seizures in SCN1A loss-of-function Dravet syndrome but benefit gain-of-function disease. This is the entry's most clinically consequential claim and is now cited rather than resting on notes.

Supports antiseizure therapy as the pharmacological cornerstone, with choice determined by syndrome and aetiology.

Action: Targeted TherapyNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is Targeted Therapy (NCIT:C93352). NCIT:C93352 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. NCIT:C93352

Identification of the specific causal gene and the functional direction of the variant (gain- versus loss-of-function) enables aetiology-directed therapy selection and is increasingly the entry point to gene-targeted treatments including antisense oligonucleotides and gene therapy.
Mechanism Target:
MODULATES Genetic Lesion in an Ion Channel or Synaptic Gene — The only entry-level treatment addressing the upstream cause rather than the seizure output. Establishing the specific gene and the functional direction of the variant redirects therapy at the lesion itself, and is the gateway to gene-targeted modalities (antisense oligonucleotides, gene therapy) still in development.

Diagnosis

1
Exome or Genome Sequencing
Genome-wide sequencing (exome or genome, ideally as a trio to enable de novo confirmation) is the first-line molecular test given the extreme genetic heterogeneity of the group. Diagnostic yield is substantially higher for seizure onset under two years of age.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:35701389 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Of the 103 patients recruited (54 males, 49 females; aged 2 weeks-17 years), the genetic aetiology was identified in 36 out of 103 (35%) with management implications in 13 out of 36."
Establishes the diagnostic yield of exome sequencing in routine clinical care of children with DEE.
PMID:35701389 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Genetic aetiology was identified in 41% of children with seizure onset under 2 years, compared to 18% with older onset."
Documents the age-of-onset dependence of diagnostic yield, informing test prioritisation.

Prevalence

Italy (15 tertiary epilepsy centres, molecular diagnoses 2012-2022)
Period Prevalence 2.6 per 100,000 1–9 per 100,000
Genetic-DEE-specific figure derived from molecularly diagnosed patients across 98 genes, accumulated over the 11-year window 2012-2022 and used by the authors as a proxy for the prevalence rate. The source calls this a "mean incidence proportion", but it is a cumulative diagnosed proportion over a defined interval rather than an annual rate, so it is recorded as PERIOD_PREVALENCE with the observation window stated here. This is a lower bound: it counts only patients who received a molecular diagnosis within the surveyed gene panel, so undiagnosed and non-panel genetic DEE are not captured.

"We included 1568 unique patients and found a mean incidence proportion of 2.6 patients for 100.000 inhabitants (SD=1.13) with consistent values across most Italian regions."
The only population-scale estimate specific to genetic DEE rather than DEE of all etiologies.

Excitatory cortical neurons from CDKL5 deficiency disorder patient-derived organoids show early hyperexcitability not identified in neurogenin2 induced neurons [Ampliseq] geo:GSE319080
CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD) is a rare developmental and epileptic encephalopathy resulting from variants in cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) that lead to impaired kinase activity or loss of function. CDD is one of the most common genetic etiologies identified in epilepsy cohorts. To study how CDKL5 variants impact human neuronal activity, gene expression and morphology, CDD patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells and their isogenic controls were differentiated into excitatory neurons using either an NGN2 induction protocol or a guided cortical organoid differentiation.

Cortical versus hippocampal network dysfunction in a human brain assembloid model of epilepsy and intellectual disability geo:GSE281622
Neurodevelopmental disorders often impair multiple cognitive domains. For instance, a genetic epilepsy syndrome might cause seizures due to cortical hyperexcitability and present with memory impairments arising from hippocampal dysfunction. This study examines how a single disorder differentially affects distinct brain regions by using human patient iPSC-derived cortical- and hippocampal-ganglionic eminence assembloids to model Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy 13 (DEE-13), a condition arising from gain-of-function mutations in the SCN8A gene.

Variability vs. phenotype: Multimodal analysis of Dravet syndrome brain organoids powered by deep learning geo:GSE256142
Dravet Syndrome (DS) is a developmental epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) driven by pathogenic variants in SCN1A gene. Brain organoids (BO) have emerged as reliable models for neurodevelopmental genetic disorders, reproducing human brain developmental milestones and rising as a promising drug testing tool. Here, we determined the underlying molecular DS pathophysiology affecting neuronal connectivity, revealing an early onset excitatory-inhibitory imbalance in maturing DS organoids circuitry. However, neuronal circuitry modeling in BO remains hampered by the notorious inter- and intra-organoid variability.

name: Genetic Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy
creation_date: "2026-07-31T00:09:41Z"
description: >-
  Genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) is a broad,
  genetically heterogeneous umbrella group of severe early-onset epilepsy
  syndromes in which pathogenic variants in any of more than nine hundred
  genes cause both refractory seizures and developmental impairment that
  exceeds what would be expected from the epileptic activity alone. Under
  the 2017 ILAE classification, "developmental and epileptic encephalopathy"
  recognizes two overlapping but separable contributors to the encephalopathy:
  a developmental component intrinsic to the underlying genetic etiology, and
  an epileptic component in which frequent seizures and epileptiform activity
  themselves worsen cognitive and behavioral outcome. Individual monogenic
  forms (numbered DEE1-DEE121+ in OMIM/MONDO, e.g. SCN1A-related Dravet
  syndrome, STXBP1 encephalopathy, KCNQ2-DEE, SCN2A-DEE, SCN8A-DEE,
  CDKL5 deficiency disorder, SYNGAP1-related DEE) are curated as their own
  dismech entries; this entry captures the mechanisms, phenotypic core, and
  clinical approach shared across the umbrella group.

  Modelling note: this is deliberately curated as an umbrella Disease rather
  than a Grouping over the gene-specific entries. A Grouping cannot carry
  pathophysiology, and the shared two-component DEE mechanism - the very thing
  that makes DEE a coherent concept - is the primary content here. The existing
  Epilepsy and Diabetes_Mellitus entries set the same precedent. Gene-specific
  detail (variant spectra, gene-specific EEG signatures, per-gene natural
  history and treatment response) belongs on the child entries, not here.
  Numbered forms that do not yet have a dismech entry of their own are
  enumerated in has_subtypes instead, each anchored to its MONDO term and to
  its causal gene, so that the concept and the gene are both recorded until a
  full entry exists. A subtype row is therefore a placeholder for a child
  entry, not a substitute for one.
